title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: At that time, as always happens, the highest society — the circles that gathered at court and at the grand balls — was divided into several groups, each with its own particular character. The largest of these was the French circle allied with Napoleon, the circle of Count Rumyantsev and Caulaincourt. In this group Helene, as soon as she had settled in Petersburg with her husband, took a very prominent place. She was visited by members of the French embassy and by many people known for their intelligence and polished manners.

Helene had been at Erfurt during the famous meeting of the Emperors and had brought back from there her connections with Napoleonic dignitaries. At Erfurt her success had been brilliant. Napoleon himself had noticed her in the theater and said of her: "That's a superb creature." Her success as a beautiful and elegant woman did not surprise Pierre, for she had become even more attractive than before. What did surprise him was that during these last two years his wife had somehow acquired the reputation of being as charming and witty as she was beautiful. The distinguished Prince de Ligne wrote her eight-page letters. Bilibin saved up his best witticisms to deliver them in Countess Bezukhova's presence. To be received in the Countess Bezukhova's salon was considered a mark of intellectual distinction. Young men read books before attending Helene's evenings so they would have something to say in her salon, and secretaries of the embassy, and even ambassadors, confided diplomatic secrets to her, so that in a way Helene became a force. Pierre, who knew she was very stupid, sometimes attended her evenings and dinner parties — where politics, poetry, and philosophy were discussed — with a strange feeling of bewilderment and dread. At these parties he felt like a conjurer who always expects his trick to be found out. But whether because stupidity was exactly what was needed to run such a salon, or because the people being deceived found pleasure in the deception, the illusion was never exposed, and Helene Bezukhova's reputation as a lovely and clever woman became so firmly established that she could say the emptiest and most foolish things and everybody would go into raptures over every word, finding deep meaning in it that she herself never intended.
* (2) "A charming woman, as witty as she is beautiful."

Pierre was exactly the kind of husband a brilliant society woman needed. He was that absent-minded eccentric, a grand nobleman of a husband who was in nobody's way and who, far from lowering the tone of the drawing room, actually enhanced it — his very contrast with his wife making her appear to better advantage. Pierre, during the last two years, as a result of his constant absorption in abstract matters and his genuine indifference to everything else, had acquired in his wife's circle — which held no interest for him — that air of ease, detachment, and goodwill toward all that cannot be faked and therefore commands real respect. He entered his wife's drawing room as one enters a theater: he knew everyone, was equally glad to see everyone, and equally indifferent to them all. Sometimes he joined in a conversation that interested him and, regardless of whether any important diplomats were present, would share his views in his slightly lisping way — views that were sometimes completely at odds with the prevailing tone. But the general opinion of the eccentric husband of "the most distinguished woman in Petersburg" was so well established that no one took his quirks seriously.

Among the many young men who visited the house every day, Boris Drubetskoy — who had already achieved considerable success in the service — was the most intimate friend of the Bezukhov household since Helene's return from Erfurt. Helene called him "my page" and treated him like a child. Her smile for him was the same as for everyone, but sometimes that smile made Pierre uncomfortable. Toward Pierre, Boris behaved with a particularly dignified and mournful deference. This shade of deference also disturbed Pierre. He had suffered so painfully three years before from the humiliation his wife had put him through that he now protected himself from any repeat, first by not being a husband to his wife in any real sense, and second by refusing to allow himself to suspect anything.

"No, now that she's become an intellectual she has finally given up her old infatuations," he told himself. "There has never been a case of a bluestocking having love affairs" — a statement which, though he'd picked it up from somewhere unknown, he believed completely. Yet strangely, Boris's constant presence in his wife's drawing room had a physical effect on Pierre: it made him stiff, constrained, and robbed him of his natural ease of movement.
"What a strange dislike," thought Pierre, "and yet I used to be quite fond of him."

In the eyes of the world Pierre was a great nobleman, the somewhat blind and foolish husband of a distinguished wife, a clever eccentric who did nothing and harmed nobody and was a thoroughly good-natured fellow. But a complex and difficult process of inner transformation was taking place all this time in Pierre's soul, revealing much to him and causing him both spiritual anguish and joy.
